blocks.text: This module opener covers what an LLM API actually is, a network accessible service letting an application send a prompt to a remote model and receive a generated response back, the dominant way applications actually access modern large language models today.

This topic covers the request and response mechanics, why the model runs as a remote service rather than local code, what a typical API call actually looks like, the tradeoffs of API-based access compared to running a model yourself, and previews what the rest of this module covers.
1. What an LLM API Actually Is

blocks.alt: Building on the completed Prompt Evaluation module, LLM APIs Fundamentals opens with what an LLM API is

blocks.text: An LLM API is a network accessible interface, typically over HTTP, that lets an application send a prompt to a language model hosted on a provider infrastructure, and receive the model generated response back, without the application needing to run the model itself.
2. Sending a Request, Receiving a Response

blocks.alt: Your application sends a request to a remote model service, which returns a response

blocks.text: At its core, using an LLM API means your application sends a request, containing the prompt and various settings, to a remote server, and receives back a response containing the model generated text, this request and response cycle is covered in much greater technical depth in the next module, API Request and Response.
3. The Model as a Remote Service, Not Local Code

blocks.alt: A model running on provider infrastructure is compared against one running locally on your own machine

blocks.text: This is a genuinely important distinction, the model itself, and the substantial computing infrastructure needed to run it, lives on the provider side, your application never actually holds the model weights or runs inference locally, it simply sends a request and waits for a response, exactly like calling any other external web service.
4. What a Typical API Call Looks Like

blocks.alt: An API key authenticates the request, the prompt gets sent as structured data, and the response comes back as structured data

blocks.text: A typical call authenticates using an API key, covered in the next few topics of this module, sends the prompt and configuration settings as structured data, usually JSON, covered in an earlier module, and receives the model response back in that same structured format.

code.content:
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.example.com/v1/chat/completions",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
    json={"model": "example-model", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]},
)

blocks.text: 5. The Provider Ecosystem

blocks.alt: Many different providers each expose their own API

blocks.text: Several different companies offer LLM APIs, each with its own specific request format, authentication approach, and available models, this course covers several of the major providers individually in dedicated modules later, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, and open source model hosting options.

blocks.text: 6. Tradeoffs of API-Based Access

blocks.alt: No infrastructure to manage yourself is weighed against reliance on the provider own uptime

blocks.text: Using an API means you never have to manage the substantial infrastructure needed to run a large model yourself, no GPUs to provision, no model weights to store, in exchange, your application performance and availability now depends on the provider own infrastructure and uptime, a genuine tradeoff covered further in the later API Production Concepts module.

blocks.title: This tradeoff mirrors a very common pattern in software generally
blocks.content: Using a managed external service instead of running infrastructure yourself is a tradeoff familiar from countless other areas of software engineering, convenience and reduced operational burden in exchange for dependency on someone else infrastructure and reliability.

blocks.text: 7. Why APIs Are the Dominant Access Pattern

For the large majority of applications, calling a hosted LLM API is dramatically simpler and cheaper than acquiring and operating the hardware needed to run a comparably capable model directly, this is exactly why API access has become the default way most applications actually integrate language model capability.
8. Every Technique From Earlier Modules Still Applies

Everything covered in the prompting-focused modules earlier in this course, prompt anatomy, structured outputs, system prompt design, still applies fully once you are actually calling a real API, this module and the ones that follow cover the practical mechanics of sending those carefully engineered prompts through an actual API call.
9. What the Rest of This Module Covers

blocks.alt: This topic is the foundation, the rest of the module covers architecture, authentication, streaming, and more

blocks.text: The remaining topics in this module cover API architecture patterns, authentication, rate limiting and quotas, SDKs, REST versus streaming APIs, and WebSockets, building the practical foundation the provider specific modules later in this course all build on.
Worked Example

A developer building their first AI powered feature initially assumes they need to somehow download and run a large language model themselves, discovering that a simple API call, sending a prompt and receiving a response over the network, is all that is actually required removes what had seemed like a major infrastructure obstacle.

Within an afternoon, they have a working prototype calling a hosted API, with all the prompt engineering techniques covered earlier in this course directly applicable to the prompt they send in that same API call.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming using a language model requires running or hosting the model yourself rather than calling a hosted API
Not accounting for the real dependency an API-based application has on the provider own uptime and reliability
Treating every provider API as interchangeable without recognizing each has its own specific request format and conventions
Forgetting that everything learned about prompt engineering in earlier modules still applies fully once calling a real API

Key Takeaway

An LLM API is a network accessible service letting an application send a prompt and receive a model generated response without running the model itself, the dominant way modern applications actually access language model capability, trading infrastructure ownership for dependency on a provider reliability, and everything covered in the prompting-focused modules earlier in this course applies directly once you are actually sending that prompt through a real API call.
